title: Conditional sentences

objectives.can: Classify a conditional sentence by the mood and particle of its 'if' clause and say what it assumes.

explanation.summary: A Greek conditional sentence announces its kind in the 'if' clause: by the particle (εἰ or ἐάν) and by the mood and tense of the verb. Learn the four patterns and you can say what the speaker is assuming, without guessing from the English.

sections.heading: Two clauses: the 'if' and the 'then'
body: A conditional sentence has an 'if' clause and a main clause. Grammarians call them the protasis and the apodosis. In Greek the protasis is introduced by εἰ (with a verb in the indicative or the optative) or by ἐάν (with a verb in the subjunctive). The little particle ἄν, which you will meet in the main clause below, is a different word.
The classification goes by form. It asks which particle and which mood the 'if' clause has, and whether the main clause has ἄν. It does not ask whether the condition is, in fact, true.

sections.heading: The four patterns
body: Traditional New Testament grammars number the patterns first to fourth class. The numbers are only labels, and other grammars use other names, so the best habit is to describe the form.

In the first pattern, εἰ with an indicative verb, the speaker takes the condition as a starting point for the argument. It does not say the condition is true. In Matthew 12:27, Jesus says εἰ ἐγὼ ἐν Βεελζεβοὺλ ἐκβάλλω τὰ δαιμόνια, 'if I cast out demons by Beelzebul', and he does not accept that this is so: he assumes it in order to show where the argument leads. In 1 Corinthians 15:13 Paul writes εἰ δὲ ἀνάστασις νεκρῶν οὐκ ἔστιν, 'if there is no resurrection of the dead', as a claim of some Corinthians that he is following out, not one that he holds.

In the second pattern, εἰ with a past indicative (imperfect, aorist or pluperfect) and ἄν in the main clause, the speaker presents the condition as not fulfilled. John 11:21 has εἰ ἦς ὧδε οὐκ ἂν ἀπέθανεν: 'if you had been here, my brother would not have died'. Martha means that Jesus was not there, and her brother did die. The imperfect usually points to the present or to a continuing state, and the aorist to a single past event.

In the third pattern, ἐάν with a subjunctive verb, the condition is open. The speaker neither assumes it nor denies it. This pattern is used for future possibilities, as in Matthew 4:9 (ἐὰν … προσκυνήσῃς), and for general cases that may happen at any time, as in 1 John 1:9 (ἐὰν ὁμολογῶμεν).

In the fourth pattern, εἰ with an optative, the condition is presented as less likely, or as a remote possibility. It is rare. In 1 Peter 3:14 and 3:17 the New Testament has εἰ with an optative (πάσχοιτε, θέλοι), but it hardly ever has the full pattern with an optative and ἄν in the main clause that older grammars describe.

'If' clause
Main clause
What it does

presents the condition as not fulfilled

a less likely or remote possibility; rare

sections.heading: Negatives and small clues
body: The negative is a clue. After εἰ with an indicative the negative is usually οὐ, as in 1 Corinthians 15:14: εἰ δὲ Χριστὸς οὐκ ἐγήγερται. After ἐάν the negative is μή, as in John 12:24: ἐὰν μὴ ὁ κόκκος … ἀποθάνῃ. Notice the verb in John 12:24: it is an aorist subjunctive, which tells you that this is the third pattern.

The tenses of the main clause are free. In John 14:28 the 'if' clause has an imperfect and the main clause an aorist with ἄν: εἰ ἠγαπᾶτέ με ἐχάρητε ἄν. The patterns are guides, not moulds, and the combination of tenses can differ. Read each clause in turn.

sections.heading: 'Assumed' is not 'true'
body: Older books sometimes say that the first pattern means 'since', or 'the condition is true'. It does not. Paul's chain of εἰ-clauses in 1 Corinthians 15:12–19 is the standard counter-example: he takes up positions he rejects, and follows them out to their consequences. A first-pattern clause means that the speaker, for the argument, treats the condition as a fact. Whether the speaker believes it is a matter for the context.

The second pattern works the same way in reverse: the form shows what the speaker takes to be the facts, which are not always the facts. In Luke 7:39 the Pharisee says εἰ ἦν προφήτης, ἐγίνωσκεν ἄν: 'if he were a prophet, he would know'. The form tells you that the Pharisee believes Jesus is not a prophet. The narrator, and the reader, may judge otherwise.

misunderstandings: Reading εἰ with an indicative as 'since' or 'because'. The clause assumes the condition for the argument; it does not assert it.
Reading ἂν in the main clause as part of the 'if' clause. In the second pattern the ἄν stands in the main clause, 'would'.
Thinking that ἐάν and εἰ are two spellings of the same word. They are different particles, and they take different moods.
Using the English 'if I were' as a sign of the second pattern. The test is the Greek: a past indicative in the 'if' clause, and usually ἄν in the main clause.

deeper.heading: Other schemes
body: The four-class scheme is convenient but not the only one. Some grammars divide conditions by their relation to time and generality (simple, general, particular, future 'more vivid' and 'less vivid'), and some by the speaker's stance. They agree about the forms and differ about how to name them. Learn the forms first, then use whichever names your grammar uses.

practice.prompt: What pattern does the 'if' clause ἐὰν … προσκυνήσῃς (words 7–9) follow?

options: εἰ with an optative
εἰ with a past indicative, with ἄν in the main clause
εἰ with a present indicative
ἐάν with a subjunctive
practice.explain: προσκυνήσῃς is an aorist subjunctive, introduced by ἐάν: the open pattern, here about the future. The second pattern needs a past indicative and the fourth an optative.

practice.prompt: In Martha's words, εἰ ἦς ὧδε οὐκ ἂν ἀπέθανεν (words 8–13), what does the form assume?

options: That Jesus was there and her brother died anyway
That Jesus was not there: the condition is presented as not fulfilled
Nothing: the form gives no hint about the facts
That Jesus might come in the future
practice.explain: A past indicative in the 'if' clause with ἄν in the main clause presents the condition as unreal. It is her view of the facts, and it turns on the imperfect ἦς, 'you were'.

practice.prompt: Jesus says εἰ ἐγὼ ἐν Βεελζεβοὺλ ἐκβάλλω τὰ δαιμόνια (words 1–5). Does the εἰ with the indicative mean that he agrees he does so?

options: No: the verb is subjunctive, so it is only a hope
No: he assumes it for the sake of the argument, which he then turns against his questioners
Yes, because the verb is present
Yes: εἰ with the indicative means 'since'
practice.explain: The first pattern takes the condition as a starting point and does not assert it. The verb ἐκβάλλω is indicative, not subjunctive, and 'since' is not what εἰ means.

practice.prompt: ἐὰν ὁμολογῶμεν (words 0–1) has a present subjunctive. What kind of condition is it?

options: A condition about the past only
A condition known to be false
A general, open condition: whenever we do this
A request addressed to God
practice.explain: ἐάν with a subjunctive is an open condition, and with a present tense it often states what holds whenever the case arises. The form does not say that anyone has confessed.

practice.prompt: ἀλλ’ εἰ καὶ πάσχοιτε (words 0–3): what is unusual about this 'if' clause?

options: It has εἰ with an optative, which is rare in the New Testament
It has ἐάν with an indicative
It has no verb
It is contrary to fact
practice.explain: πάσχοιτε is an optative. The fourth pattern is rare and presents a remote possibility, 'even if you should suffer'. The clause is not contrary to fact, because that would need a past indicative.

check.prompt: Paul writes εἰ δὲ ἀνάστασις νεκρῶν οὐκ ἔστιν (words 0–5). What does the εἰ with the indicative do here?

options: It makes the claim a future possibility
It asserts that there is no resurrection
It says the claim is false, as a contrary-to-fact condition
It takes up a claim, quoted in the previous verse, as a starting point for the argument
check.explain: The first pattern assumes the condition for the argument. Paul disagrees with it, as the next verses show. Contrary to fact would need a past indicative and ἄν.

check.prompt: εἰ ὁ θεὸς πατὴρ ὑμῶν ἦν, ἠγαπᾶτε ἂν ἐμέ (words 4–11): what are the clues to the pattern?

options: ἐάν with a subjunctive
εἰ with an imperfect, and ἄν in the main clause with another imperfect
εἰ with an optative
εἰ with a present indicative and no ἄν
check.explain: ἦν and ἠγαπᾶτε are imperfects, and ἄν is in the main clause: the second pattern. The imperfect refers here to the present, 'if God were your father, you would love me', which assumes he is not.

check.prompt: ὅτι εἰ ἐν Τύρῳ καὶ Σιδῶνι ἐγένοντο αἱ δυνάμεις (words 6–13) … πάλαι ἂν … μετενόησαν (words 20–25): what do the aorist indicatives and ἄν show?

options: A condition about the future
The deeds were not done in Tyre and Sidon, and so those cities did not repent
A first-pattern condition that is true
The cities repented, and the deeds were done there
check.explain: The second pattern with aorists refers to an unreal past: if the deeds had been done there, they would have repented. It implies they were not done there, and those cities did not repent.

check.prompt: ἐάν τις τὸν ἐμὸν λόγον τηρήσῃ (words 3–9): which mood does the 'if' clause have, and what does it do?

quoted.title: John
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. options: Indicative: it asserts that someone keeps the word
Subjunctive: it states an open condition that any person may meet
Imperative: it gives a command
Optative: it states a wish
check.explain: τηρήσῃ is an aorist subjunctive after ἐάν. The condition is open and general ('anyone who …'). It does not claim that someone has kept the word.

check.prompt: The Pharisee thinks εἰ ἦν προφήτης, ἐγίνωσκεν ἄν (words 12–16). What does the form tell us?

options: That in his view Jesus is not a prophet
That Jesus certainly is not a prophet
That the Pharisee is unsure whether Jesus is a prophet
That Jesus will become a prophet
check.explain: Imperfects with ἄν mark a condition presented as unreal. The form tells us about the speaker's assumption, not about the truth: the narrator and the reader may judge otherwise.

check.prompt: ἐὰν μὴ ὁ κόκκος … ἀποθάνῃ (words 3–14): what does the μή and the verb form tell you?

quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. options: A second-pattern condition: the verb is a past indicative
A third-pattern condition: ἐάν with a subjunctive takes μή
A fourth-pattern condition: the verb is an optative
A first-pattern condition: εἰ and an indicative would have οὐ
check.explain: ἀποθάνῃ is an aorist subjunctive, and ἐάν goes with μή. An εἰ-clause with an indicative would usually have οὐ for its negative, as in 1 Corinthians 15:14.

check.prompt: κρεῖττον γὰρ ἀγαθοποιοῦντας, εἰ θέλοι τὸ θέλημα τοῦ θεοῦ, πάσχειν (words 0–9): how is εἰ θέλοι classified?

quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. options: A first-pattern condition, with an indicative
A fourth-pattern condition: εἰ with an optative, a remote possibility
A third-pattern condition, with a subjunctive
A second-pattern condition, with a past indicative
check.explain: θέλοι is a present optative. The clause treats the matter as a remote possibility: 'if the will of God should so wish'. The main clause has no matching optative.

check.prompt: εἰ ἠγαπᾶτέ με ἐχάρητε ἄν (words 10–14): what makes this a condition presented as unreal?

quoted.title: John
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. options: The optative in the main clause
The pronoun με
The past indicative ἠγαπᾶτε in the εἰ clause, together with ἄν in the main clause
The word ἄν alone, wherever it stands
check.explain: A past indicative in the 'if' clause with ἄν in the main clause is the second pattern. Here the tenses are mixed (imperfect, then aorist), which is allowed. The particle ἄν also appears in other constructions, so by itself it is not enough.

reading.why: Eight verses of εἰ-clauses in a chain. Paul assumes a claim for the argument, follows out its consequences and rejects it. They show how the first pattern works in a real argument.
